questions.prompt: Consider ℝ with its usual topology. Which assertion is correct?

options.A: A finite set containing 33 elements has at least 3 different Hausdorff topologies.
options.B: Let X be a nonempty finite set with a Hausdorff topology. On X×X with the product topology, every function f:X×X→ℝ is continuous.
options.C: Let X be an infinite discrete topological space. If f:ℝ→X is continuous and g:X→ℝ is any nonconstant function, the range of g∘f contains at least 2 elements.
options.D: If a nonempty metric space X has a finite dense subset, there exists a discontinuous function f:X→ℝ.

hints: Show that singletons are open in a finite Hausdorff space.
Use connectedness of ℝ for the third assertion, and closedness of finite sets for the fourth.
questions.solution: A finite Hausdorff space is discrete: for x, choose neighborhoods separating x from every other point and intersect the finitely many neighborhoods of x. Thus its only Hausdorff topology is the discrete topology, refuting A. The product X×X is discrete, so every inverse image is open and B holds. A continuous image of connected ℝ in a discrete space is a singleton, so g∘f is constant even when g is nonconstant; C fails. A finite set in a metric space is closed; if it is dense it equals X. Finite metric spaces are discrete and all real-valued functions on them are continuous, refuting D.
questions.theory: A space is Hausdorff when any two distinct points have disjoint neighborhoods. Hausdorff spaces are T₁: each singleton is closed. On a finite T₁ space, every subset is a finite union of closed singletons and therefore closed, so every subset is also open. Consequently the finite Hausdorff topology is uniquely discrete. Products of finitely many discrete spaces are discrete, and every function with discrete domain is continuous. Connectedness is preserved by continuous maps, while a connected subset of a discrete space has at most one point. Finally finite subsets of metric spaces are closed, so a finite dense subset forces the whole space to be finite. Density alone does not mean the topology is indiscrete; the separation hypothesis determines this conclusion.

similar_questions.prompt: Prove that every function from a three-point Hausdorff space into ℝ is continuous.
similar_questions.solution: Every singleton is closed; finiteness makes every subset closed and open. Inverse images of open sets are subsets of this discrete domain, hence open.

similar_questions.prompt: Can a continuous f:ℝ→ℤ, where ℤ has the discrete topology, take two values?
similar_questions.solution: No. ℝ is connected, so f(ℝ) is connected. If it contained distinct integers, one singleton and its complement would separate it. Hence f is constant.

questions.prompt: Let f:ℝ²→ℝ be locally Lipschitz. For ẋ=f(t,x), x(t₀)=x₀, let J(t₀,x₀) be the maximal interval of existence. Which statement is true?
hints: Local existence applies around every finite point of a solution.
A finite included endpoint would permit extending the solution past that endpoint.
questions.solution: Local Lipschitz continuity gives a unique solution on a neighborhood of t₀, so J is nonempty. At any finite time where the solution has a finite value, local existence extends it to both sides. Therefore the maximal interval contains neither finite endpoint and is open, proving B. Global existence is not guaranteed: ẋ=x², x(0)=1 has solution x=1/(1−t) on (−∞,1), refuting A and the universal assertion C. D contradicts local existence. Some maximal intervals equal ℝ and are also closed, but closedness is not guaranteed for every IVP.
questions.theory: Picard–Lindelöf gives local existence and uniqueness when the right-hand side is continuous in time and locally Lipschitz in the state; joint local Lipschitz continuity is a stronger sufficient condition. Compatible local solutions unite into a unique maximal solution on an open interval containing the initial time. A finite endpoint can only obstruct continuation when the solution leaves every compact subset of the domain. On the full plane, a bounded state near a finite endpoint would permit continuation, so finite-time blow-up is the relevant obstruction. Local Lipschitz continuity does not imply a global growth bound and therefore does not ensure existence for all time. Global Lipschitz or suitable linear growth assumptions can supply global existence. Remember that ℝ itself is both open and closed; the universally valid property here is openness.

similar_questions.solution: Separating gives −1/x=t−1/2, hence x=2/(1−2t). Its pole is at t=1/2; the maximal interval containing 0 is (−∞,1/2).

similar_questions.solution: The solution is x(t)=4e^{−(t−3)}, finite and differentiable for every real t. Its maximal interval is ℝ.

questions.theory: For a constant matrix A, the unique solution of ẋ=Ax is e^{tA}x₀. If A has distinct real eigenvalues, its eigenvectors form a basis and the solution decomposes into independent exponential modes. A claim for every nonzero initial state must include data in the eigenspace of the slowest eigenvalue, as well as combinations containing the fastest mode. Multiplying by e^{−ct} shifts every exponential growth rate by −c. Thus c greater than the largest eigenvalue forces decay, but equality generally leaves a nonzero limiting vector. Positive eigenvalues preclude bounded nonzero forward solutions in this diagonalizable example. Any norm on a finite-dimensional vector space gives the same convergence and boundedness conclusions, because such norms are equivalent. Defective matrices require additional polynomial factors from Jordan blocks.

questions.prompt: Let u solve the Cauchy problem uuₓ+uᵧ=0 for x∈ℝ,y>0, with u(x,0)=x. Find u(2,3).

questions.theory: The method of characteristics converts a first-order quasilinear PDE a(x,y,u)uₓ+b(x,y,u)uᵧ=c(x,y,u) into the ODEs x′=a, y′=b, u′=c. Cauchy data specify starting points and values on an initial curve. To recover a classical solution, the characteristic parametrization must be locally invertible and the initial curve must be noncharacteristic. For uᵧ+u uₓ=0, the value of u stays constant along each straight characteristic, whose slope depends on that value. Characteristics can intersect for other initial data, causing a gradient singularity or shock. Here x=ξ(1+y) is invertible for y>0, giving a smooth global forward solution. Substituting the result into both the PDE and initial data checks signs and the denominator.

Orthogonality makes the modes independent. In this question L=2, and the displayed modes correspond to n=2 and n=4 rather than the first two eigenfunctions. questions.prompt: Which values give degree of precision 3 for ∫_{−1}¹f(x)dx≈a f(−1)+b f(1)+c f′(−1)+d f′(1)?
hints: Require exactness for 1,x,x²,x³.

questions.solution: Testing 1,x,x²,x³ yields a+b=2, −a+b+c+d=0, a+b−2c+2d=2/3, and −a+b+3c+3d=0. Subtracting the odd equations gives c+d=0, then a=b=1. The quadratic equation gives −2c+2d=−4/3, hence c=1/3,d=−1/3. This is A. For x⁴, the formula gives 2−4/3−4/3=−2/3, whereas the exact integral is2/5; precision is exactly3. B,D fail on constants, and C fails on x².
questions.theory: The degree of precision of a quadrature rule is the largest integer m for which it integrates every polynomial of degree at most m exactly. Linearity means that checking the monomial basis 1,x,…,x^m is sufficient. A derivative-based rule is a Hermite-type quadrature: values and derivatives impose different moment equations, and derivative signs at a negative node must be computed carefully. Symmetry often forces equal endpoint-value weights and opposite endpoint-derivative weights. Satisfying m+1 equations proves precision at least m, but an additional monomial is needed to exclude higher precision. Such rules approximate smooth general functions but need not have positive derivative weights. Never infer precision solely from the number of coefficients; solve the moment system and check the next degree.

questions.prompt: Consider J(y)=∫₀¹[(y′)²−y|y|y′+xy]dx with y(0)=y(1)=0. Which statement about its stationary functions is correct?

options.B: y≡0 is the only stationary function.
options.C: There is a unique stationary function y not identically zero.
options.D: There are infinitely many stationary functions.

hints: The term y|y|y′ is the derivative of |y|³/3.
With fixed zero endpoints, that term integrates to zero; apply Euler–Lagrange to (y′)²+xy.
questions.solution: Since d(|y|³/3)/dx=y|y|y′ and both endpoint values are zero, J(y)=∫₀¹[(y′)²+xy]dx. For variations η vanishing at the endpoints, δJ=∫(2y′η′+xη)dx=∫(−2y″+x)η dx. Stationarity requires y″=x/2. Integrating gives y=x³/12+C₁x+C₂; endpoints give C₂=0,C₁=−1/12. Thus y=(x³−x)/12 is the unique extremal, nonzero on (0,1), proving C. A,D contradict uniqueness and existence; B fails because its first variation is ∫xη dx, generally nonzero.
questions.theory: A stationary function makes the first variation vanish for every admissible variation. With fixed endpoints, variations vanish there, so integration by parts leads to the Euler–Lagrange equation ∂L/∂y−d(∂L/∂y′)/dx=0. Adding a total derivative to an integrand changes the functional only by an endpoint term; it does not change fixed-endpoint stationarity. The absolute value here causes no difficulty because |y|³ is continuously differentiable and its derivative is3y|y|. Solving the resulting boundary-value equation identifies all stationary functions. Stationarity alone generally does not imply minimality, but the reduced functional is strictly convex in the derivative: for a nonzero zero-endpoint variation, its second variation is2∫(η′)²>0. This additionally makes the unique extremal the unique minimizer.

similar_questions.solution: Euler–Lagrange gives2−2y″=0, so y=x²+ax+b. Endpoints imply b=0,a=−1; y=x²−x is the unique extremal.

questions.solution: For −y″=f with Dirichlet endpoints, the Green function is K(x,t)=t(1−x) when t<x and x(1−t) when t>x. It vanishes at x=0,1, is continuous at x=t, and Kₓ(t+,t)−Kₓ(t−,t)=−t−(1−t)=−1. Thus −∂ₓ²K=δ_t and y=∫K f. Substituting f=2y gives the displayed equation, proving A. questions.theory: A Green function represents the inverse of a differential operator subject to boundary conditions. For the Dirichlet operator L=−d²/dx² on [0,1], the homogeneous equation gives linear pieces to either side of the source point. Endpoint conditions set one piece proportional to x and the other to1−x. Continuity prevents a derivative-of-delta term, and a first-derivative jump of−1 creates the unit delta under L. The resulting symmetric kernel is min(x,t)[1−max(x,t)]. Replacing a differential equation Ly=λy by y=λ∫K y creates a Fredholm integral equation. The sign depends on whether L is y″ or−y″; it must be tracked rather than memorized. Values on a single diagonal do not matter for ordinary integration, though continuity gives the natural definition.

questions.theory: Canonical coordinates preserve Hamilton’s equations and the symplectic two-form dq∧dp. A constant new momentum cannot form a coordinate system because its Jacobian vanishes. Power transformations must be assessed on a domain where all powers are defined and smooth; the correct transformation here uses1/q and excludes q=0. Checking the bracket both proves local preservation and establishes nonzero Jacobian, while an explicit inverse confirms invertibility on each component.

questions.prompt: Let X₁,…,X₄ be iid Bernoulli(1/3), with order statistics X₍₁₎≤⋯≤X₍₄₎. Which assertion is true?

It is Bernoulli with parameter P(Binomial(4,1/3)≥3).
questions.solution: X₍₂₎=1 iff at least3 of the4 observations equal1. Its success probability is4(1/3)³(2/3)+(1/3)⁴=9/81=1/9. Therefore its expectation is1/9 and variance(1/9)(8/9)=8/81, proving C and refuting B. The minimum equals1 only when all observations are1, with probability1/81; then the maximum is necessarily1. But P(maximum=1)=1−(2/3)⁴=65/81<1, so the extremes are dependent, refuting A. Since the maximum has positive probabilities at both0 and1, it is not degenerate, refuting D.
questions.theory: Order statistics are sample values arranged in increasing order, including repetitions. For a Bernoulli sample of size n, the kth smallest value is1 exactly when at most k−1 zeros occur, equivalently when the number of ones is at least n−k+1. Thus each order statistic is Bernoulli, although different order statistics are usually dependent. A Bernoulli variable with success probability q has expectation q and variance q(1−q), because its square equals itself. Extremes have simple probabilities: the minimum is1 with probability pⁿ, and the maximum is0 with probability(1−p)ⁿ. A random variable is degenerate only when one value has probability one. Independence of the original observations does not pass automatically to their sorted values, which use overlapping information.

The unique closest allowed value is5, so the MLE is5, B. Values6 and9 are outside the parameter space; μ=3 is allowed but has lower likelihood than5. Equivalently the log-likelihood derivative is18−3μ>0 throughout μ≤5, so its maximum is attained at the included endpoint.
questions.theory: A maximum likelihood estimator maximizes the likelihood over the specified parameter space, not over an unconstrained enlargement. For a normal sample with known variance, completing the square reduces the optimization to minimizing the squared distance between the parameter and the sample mean. On a closed interval this is the projection, or clipping, of the sample mean onto that interval. A boundary maximum need not have derivative zero; the derivative condition applies only to interior optima. Inclusion of the boundary matters: if μ<5 rather than μ≤5, this sample’s likelihood would have a supremum as μ approaches5 but no maximizing parameter. The MLE is a function of the observed sample and respects all model constraints even when the empirical mean does not.

questions.prompt: Let X be Poisson with mean λ. Which parametric function is not estimable?

questions.solution: Here estimable means admitting an integrable unbiased estimator for every λ>0. X estimates λ, X(X−1) estimates λ² by the factorial moment identity, and1_{X=0} estimates e^{−λ}. Suppose Eλ[g(X)]=1/λ. Then Σ_{k≥0}g(k)λ^k/k!=e^λ/λ. Integrability at any λ₀>0 ensures absolute convergence of the left series for0≤λ≤λ₀, so its limit as λ↓0 is the finite number g(0). The right side diverges. This contradiction rules out unbiased estimation of λ^{−1}, so A is correct. The conclusion concerns unbiased estimation, not whether one can propose a biased estimator or obtain consistency from growing samples.
questions.theory: A parametric function is unbiasedly estimable when some statistic with finite expectation has that function as its expectation at every parameter value. For a Poisson observation, Eλ[g(X)]=e^{−λ}Σg(k)λ^k/k!, so admissible expectation functions are linked to exponential generating series. Integrability for each positive λ forces these series to be locally absolutely convergent, including continuity toward zero. A target with a nonremovable singularity at zero, such as1/λ, cannot arise in this way. Poisson factorial moments satisfy E[(X)ᵣ]=λʳ, where(X)ᵣ=X(X−1)⋯(X−r+1), giving polynomial targets explicit estimators. The event X=0 has probability e^{−λ}. The term estimable is used here in this standard unbiased sense; ordinary point estimation does not require unbiasedness and would pose a different question.

questions.prompt: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid N(θ,1), θ∈ℝ. With X̄=n^{−1}ΣXᵢ and t_{0.975,n−1} the 0.975 quantile of Student t with n−1 degrees of freedom, consider X̄±t_{0.975,n−1}/√n. Which statement is true?

options.C: Its confidence level is more than0.95.

hints: The variance is known, so √n(X̄−θ) is standard normal, not Student t.
For finite positive degrees of freedom, the upper0.975 t quantile exceeds the corresponding normal quantile.
questions.solution: For n≥2, Z=√n(X̄−θ)∼N(0,1). The interval covers θ iff|Z|≤t_{0.975,n−1}, so coverage is2Φ(t_{0.975,n−1})−1. For finiteν=n−1, t_{0.975,ν}>z_{0.975}; therefore coverage is strictly greater than2Φ(z_{0.975})−1=0.95, proving C. Student t calibration yields exact95% coverage when the unknown standard deviation is estimated and its sample value multiplies the critical value. That is not the displayed known-variance interval. A is only the limiting coverage as n→∞; B reverses the comparison and D is false because it is a valid conservative confidence interval.
questions.theory: A confidence interval has confidence level equal to its repeated-sampling coverage probability, computed under the model. For iid normal observations with known varianceσ², √n(X̄−θ)/σ has an exact standard normal law. Ifσ is unknown and replaced by the sample standard deviation S, the pivot √n(X̄−θ)/S has Student t distribution with n−1 degrees of freedom. Student t has larger positive upper quantiles than the standard normal at conventional central confidence levels, reflecting uncertainty in variance estimation. Using a t critical value with the known standard deviation therefore makes the interval wider and conservative. The true parameter is fixed in the frequentist coverage calculation; randomness comes from the interval. The notation requires n≥2 because a Student t law with zero degrees of freedom is undefined.

questions.prompt: Samples X₁,…,X₇ and Y₁,…,Y₉ are independent with continuous CDFs F,G. For the Wald–Wolfowitz runs test of H₀:F=G against inequality somewhere, let R count runs in the pooled ordered label sequence. Which pair is correct?

Count positive compositions of7 and9 into the specified numbers of alternating runs.
questions.solution: There are C(16,7)=11440 equally likely label sequences. For R=6 there are3 runs of each label; either label can start. The count is2C(6,2)C(8,2)=840, so probability840/11440=21/286. For R=9, one label has5 runs and the other4. The count is C(6,4)C(8,3)+C(6,3)C(8,4)=15·56+20·70=2240, giving2240/11440=28/143. Hence C. A has the wrong even-run probability, and B,D have the wrong odd-run probability. Their duplication does not affect the uniquely correct option.
questions.theory: A run is a maximal consecutive block of identical labels in an ordered sequence. Under equal continuous distributions, pooled observations have no ties almost surely, and exchangeability makes all arrangements with the fixed label counts equally probable. A positive composition of m items into k runs has C(m−1,k−1) choices. For two sample sizes m,n, an even number2k of runs has2C(m−1,k−1)C(n−1,k−1) arrangements. An odd number2k+1 has C(m−1,k)C(n−1,k−1)+C(m−1,k−1)C(n−1,k) arrangements. Divide these counts by C(m+n,m). The factor2 belongs to the even case because either label may start and end differently. The odd case already separates which label occupies both endpoints. Ties require an additional procedure rather than the continuous null formula.

similar_questions.solution: There are C(4,2)=6 sequences. Only XXYY and YYXX have2 runs, so probability2/6=1/3.

similar_questions.solution: Odd-run formula with k=1 gives C(2,1)C(1,0)+C(2,0)C(1,1)=3 arrangements. There are C(5,3)=10 sequences, so probability3/10.

hints: Divide by xᵢ when xᵢ≠0 to obtain equal-variance observations of β.

A linear unbiased estimator ΣaᵢZᵢ requiresΣaᵢ=1 and has varianceσ²Σaᵢ²≥σ²/n, with equality exactly when each aᵢ=1/n. Thus the BLUE is(1/n)ΣYᵢ/xᵢ. Hence the printed Part B single-answer item has two correct labels under its intended nonzero-design assumption, and cannot be graded uniquely. The source does not state xᵢ≠0; if some xᵢ=0 the displayed divisions are undefined and the zero-design observations contain no information aboutβ. If all are zero, β is unidentifiable. A,B are generally unbiased when defined but not minimum-variance for unequal designs.
questions.theory: The Gauss–Markov principle characterizes the minimum-variance linear unbiased estimator under a specified covariance matrix; normality is unnecessary. In a model through the origin with unequal error variances, generalized least squares weights observation i by the inverse variance. Here dividing by nonzero xᵢ produces uncorrelated observations all with meanβ and varianceσ², so their equal-weight average is optimal by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality. The ordinary least-squares expression is optimal under equal original variances, which is a different assumption. Algebraically identical options remain two correct choices even if written in different forms. The nonzero-design hypothesis is necessary for the printed ratios and for an invertible covariance matrix; zero design points should be omitted, with the effective number of informative observations replacing n. A single-answer source must distinguish its options to support unique grading.

The sum of all entries in Q equals(X₁+X₂)²+(X₃+X₄)².
questions.solution: The block covariance I₂⊗Σ gives two independent rows with common covarianceΣ. The sum S of all Q entries is(X₁+X₂)²+(X₃+X₄)². Each row sum is centered normal with variance2+2+2(−1)=2, and the row sums are independent. Thus S=2(U₁²+U₂²) for independent standard normals, i.e.2χ₂². A univariate Wishart W₁(n,s) is sχ_n², so S∼W₁(2,2), A. B has one degree of freedom, C has scale1, and D has four degrees of freedom. The four original coordinates do not yield four independent squared terms in this scalar quadratic form.
questions.theory: A Wishart matrix Wₘ(n,Σ) is the sum of n independent outer products of centered m-dimensional normal vectors with covarianceΣ. For any fixed vector a, aᵀQa is the sum of n squared independent normal variables with variance aᵀΣa, hence has distribution(aᵀΣa)χ_n². In dimension one this is W₁(n,aᵀΣa). A Kronecker covariance I_n⊗Σ encodes independent normal blocks with within-block covarianceΣ, provided the vectorization order matches those blocks. Here the explicit row arrangement makes that match visible. The total sum of matrix entries is1ᵀQ1, not its trace. Off-diagonal covariance terms affect the projection variance and cannot be discarded. Degrees of freedom count independent rows contributing to the projected sum, rather than the total number of entries.

Multivariate normal distributions are closed under affine transformations, including singular transformations that may give degenerate normal laws. Covariance matrices must be symmetric and positive semidefinite; these properties are preserved byAΣAᵀ. Computing individual entries can be faster in a diagonal scaling problem, but matrix multiplication provides a reliable check for general mixtures of coordinates.

questions.prompt: Let xₙ>0 and σₙ=(x₁+⋯+xₙ)/n. Which statements are true? lim sup denotes limit supremum.

options.A: If limsup xₙ=ℓ and(xₙ) is decreasing, then limsup σₙ=ℓ.
options.B: limsup xₙ=ℓ if and only if limsup σₙ=ℓ.
options.C: If limsup n(xₙ/xₙ₊₁−1)<1, then Σxₙ converges.
options.D: If limsup n(xₙ/xₙ₊₁−1)<1, then Σxₙ diverges.

hints: A positive decreasing sequence converges, and its Cesàro means share its limit.
The ratio expression is Raabe’s test; below1 it forces divergence.
questions.solution: A positive decreasing sequence converges to its infimumℓ; Cesàro’s theorem givesσₙ→ℓ, proving A. B is false: alternate xₙ=1 and2; then limsup xₙ=2 butσₙ→3/2. For D choose0<r<1 above the given limsup. Eventually xₙ/xₙ₊₁≤1+r/n, hence xₙ₊₁≥xₙ/(1+r/n). Iterating and using log(1+r/n)≤r/n gives xₙ≥C n^{−r} for a constant C>0. Since r<1, the comparison series diverges, proving D. C is false, for example xₙ=1 gives the ratio expression0 yetΣxₙ diverges. Thus A,D are correct.
questions.theory: Cesàro’s theorem states that the arithmetic means of a convergent real sequence converge to the same limit. A positive decreasing sequence is bounded below and therefore convergent, so its limsup is its ordinary limit. For general oscillating sequences, averaging can change the limsup and even create a limit when the original sequence has none. Raabe’s test refines the ratio test through Rₙ=n(aₙ/aₙ₊₁−1) for positive terms. If liminf Rₙ>1, the series converges; if limsup Rₙ<1, it diverges. Strict inequalities are essential because the threshold case can go either way. The divergence proof compares terms with n^{−r} for some r<1 using a product estimate. No monotonicity assumption on the general positive terms is required for that implication.

similar_questions.prompt: Apply Raabe’s test to aₙ=n^{−p} for p>0.
similar_questions.solution: Rₙ=n[(1+1/n)^p−1]→p. Thus p>1 gives convergence and p<1 gives divergence. At p=1 the test is inconclusive, though the harmonic series diverges.

questions.prompt: Under which conditions is a real sequence(xₙ) convergent?

options.A: The subsequences(x₂ₙ₊₁),(x₂ₙ),(x₃ₙ) converge and have the same limit.
options.C: For every integer k≥2, the subsequence(xₖₙ)ₙ converges.

For the third condition, try exceptional terms at prime indices.
questions.solution: A is sufficient because eventually both parities are arbitrarily close to the same limit. For B let the even, odd and multiples-of3 limits be L_e,L_o,L_3. The shared subsequence x₆ₙ gives L_e=L_3, while x₆ₙ₊₃ gives L_o=L_3; hence both parity limits coincide and the whole sequence converges. C is false: take xₙ=1 when n is prime and0 otherwise. For each fixed k≥2, kn is composite for n≥2, so xₖₙ→0. Yet infinitely many primes and composites give distinct subsequential limits1 and0. D is false: xₙ=log(n+1) diverges while log((n+2)/(n+1))→0. Therefore A,B.
questions.theory: A sequence converges exactly when all sufficiently late terms become close to one finite value. If its indices are partitioned into finitely many subsequences, convergence of each to the same limit implies convergence of the whole sequence by taking the maximum of their finitely many cutoff indices. Convergence of the pieces to different limits is insufficient, but an additional subsequence overlapping each piece infinitely often can force equality by uniqueness of limits. The multiples-of3 subsequence connects the even and odd pieces here. An infinite family of convergent subsequences need not control uncovered or sparsely covered indices: prime-index spikes escape every fixed multiples-of-k tail. Finally successive differences tending to zero is necessary for convergence but is much weaker than the Cauchy property, which controls every pair of late terms.

questions.theory: Continuity of a restriction uses the subspace topology: only nearby points belonging to the chosen subset are relevant. Sequential continuity in a metric subspace requires f(xₙ)→f(x) for every sequence of points in that subspace tending to x. Isolated points impose no obstacle because a small relative neighborhood consists of that point alone. For the reciprocal-integer subset, zero is non-isolated but all function values are zero, so continuity there is immediate. An accumulation point outside the domain does not itself require a value or continuity condition. This distinguishes continuity from possible extension to the closure and from uniform continuity.

Heine–Cantor proves B. On V, x=y and z=w imply xw−yz=xz−xz=0; constant functions are uniformly continuous, proving C even though V is unbounded. For D, the points(t,0,0,−t) belong to W since their coordinate sum is0, and f=−t²→−∞. Also(t,−2t,0,t) lies in W and gives f=t²→∞. Thus f is unbounded and every option is true.
questions.theory: Polynomials in finitely many real variables are continuous because sums and products preserve continuity. Heine–Borel identifies compact subsets of Euclidean space as closed and bounded; Heine–Cantor then makes every continuous function on such a set uniformly continuous. Polynomial equality constraints define closed sets, but their boundedness must be checked separately. A restriction to an unbounded set may still be uniformly continuous, especially if the defining constraints make the function constant. A bound on one linear combination of coordinates does not bound the coordinates individually, since positive and negative terms can cancel. To show a function unbounded, produce a sequence in the set whose values have unbounded magnitude; unboundedness of the set alone is insufficient. Both positive and negative constructions are available here.

Nonnegative integrability does imply the areas of the tails tend to zero, but this is a statement about mass rather than every function value. Stronger assumptions such as uniform continuity can preclude persistent narrow spikes. When disproving a universal assertion, one explicit continuous nonnegative counterexample can settle several related claims.

questions.prompt: Let μ be Lebesgue measure and μ* its outer measure on ℝ. For nonempty A⊂[0,1], which statements are true?

options.A: If the interior and closure of A have the same outer measure, A is Lebesgue measurable.
options.B: If A is open, it is Lebesgue measurable and μ(A)>0.
options.C: If A is not Lebesgue measurable, the irrational numbers in A have positive outer measure.
options.D: If μ*(A)=0, then A has empty interior.

hints: Open and closed sets are measurable; compare the closure with the interior.
Every subset of a null set is Lebesgue measurable, and the rationals form a null set.
questions.solution: Write U=int A,F=closure A. Both are measurable with finite measures. If μ*(U)=μ*(F), then μ(F∖U)=0. Since U⊂A⊂F, A differs from U by a subset of a null set; completeness gives measurability, proving A. A nonempty open subset ofℝ contains a nondegenerate interval, giving positive measure and proving B. If μ*(A∖ℚ)=0, then A∖ℚ is measurable null; A∩ℚ is also measurable null because countable. Their union A would be measurable, so a nonmeasurable A must have μ*(A∖ℚ)>0, proving C. Nonempty interior contains an interval with positive outer measure; hence null outer measure forces empty interior, proving D.
questions.theory: Lebesgue outer measure is defined for every subset, whereas Lebesgue measure is its restriction to measurable sets. Open and closed subsets ofℝ are Borel and therefore measurable. Lebesgue measure is complete: any subset of a measure-zero measurable set is itself measurable with measure zero. Consequently any set of outer measure zero is measurable. For bounded measurable U⊂F, equality of their measures gives μ(F∖U)=0 by finite additivity. A set trapped between them is then measurable, even if it is not Borel. Every nonempty open set contains an interval and has positive measure, but the converse fails: a positive-measure set can have empty interior. Countable sets, especiallyℚ, are null; removing them cannot account for nonmeasurability.

similar_questions.solution: The only possible extra points are0 and1, a finite null set. Thus A differs from the measurable interval by a null subset and is measurable with measure1.

similar_questions.prompt: Does empty interior imply zero Lebesgue measure?
similar_questions.solution: No. Starting with[0,1], at stage k remove a middle open interval of length4^{−k} from each of the2^{k−1} remaining components. The removed intervals are disjoint and their total length isΣ_{k≥1}2^{k−1}4^{−k}=1/2. The closed remaining set thus has measure1/2. Its component lengths tend to0 and the removed intervals occur at every scale, so it contains no interval and has empty interior.

At zero, [g(h)−g(0)]/h=|h|^{2/3}/h has magnitude|h|^{−1/3} and diverges, with opposite signs on the two sides. Thus g is not differentiable at0 on a nondegenerate interval containing0; C,D are false. questions.theory: The implicit function theorem states that a continuously differentiable F(x,y) with F(x₀,y₀)=0 and nonzero derivative F_y(x₀,y₀) locally defines a unique continuously differentiable y=g(x). When the derivative vanishes, the theorem gives no conclusion: a continuous unique branch may still exist, differentiability may fail, or there may be several branches. Direct algebra settles x²=y³ because the real cube function is one-to-one and onto. The resulting cusp y=|x|^{2/3} is continuous but has unbounded difference quotients at zero. A vertical tangent in the plane is consistent with continuity as a graph and failure of a finite derivative. Existence, uniqueness, continuity and differentiability are separate properties; checking one does not establish the others.

If a gradient is nonzero, substitute y=x+t∇f(x) and let t grow.
questions.solution: For z=(1−t)x+ty with0≤t≤1, apply the hypothesis at z to x and y. Multiplying by1−t andt and adding cancels the gradient terms, yielding(1−t)f(x)+tf(y)≥f(z). Hence f is convex, B. The example f(x)=|x|² satisfies the inequality because the difference equals|y−x|², yet is neither constant nor bounded; A,C fail. If f is bounded above and ∇f(x)≠0 somewhere, setting y=x+s∇f(x) gives f(y)≥f(x)+s|∇f(x)|²→∞, contradiction. Thus a bounded f has zero gradient everywhere and is constant on connectedℝⁿ, proving D.
questions.theory: A function on a convex domain is convex when f((1−t)x+ty)≤(1−t)f(x)+tf(y) for all0≤t≤1. For differentiable functions this is equivalent to every tangent affine hyperplane lying below the graph, the inequality in the question. For C² functions it is also equivalent to the Hessian being positive semidefinite everywhere, but no Hessian computation is needed here. On the full space, a nonzero gradient gives a ray along which the supporting affine function grows unboundedly; therefore a convex differentiable function bounded above is constant. Bounded below alone is insufficient, as|x|² shows. The full unbounded domain matters: a nonconstant convex function can be bounded on a bounded domain. Convexity also makes any stationary point a global minimizer.

questions.prompt: For an arbitrary normed linear space U, which statements are true?

options.A: Every bounded linear functional U→ℝ is continuous.
options.B: U is isomorphic to its double dual U**.
options.D: The closed unit ball of U is compact.

hints: A bounded linear map obeys|f(x)|≤C‖x‖.
Hahn–Banach supplies a norm-one functional attaining‖x‖ at any nonzero x; compact unit balls require finite dimension.
questions.solution: A bounded linear functional satisfies|f(x)−f(y)|=|f(x−y)|≤‖f‖‖x−y‖ and is continuous, so A holds. The upper bound in C follows from the dual norm. For x≠0, define a functional on span{x} by g(tx)=t‖x‖; it has norm1. Hahn–Banach extends it to f∈U* with‖f‖=1 and f(x)=‖x‖, proving equality. B is false: U=c₀ is separable, but U**≅ℓ∞ is not separable, so they are not isomorphic as normed spaces. D is false inℓ² because its unit vectors lie in the unit ball with pairwise distance√2 and no convergent subsequence. Thus A,C.
questions.theory: A linear functional is bounded when it is bounded on the unit ball, equivalently when|f(x)|≤C‖x‖ for every x. This is equivalent to continuity and defines the operator norm. The continuous dual U* consists of these functionals, and the canonical map J:U→U** sends x to evaluation Jx(f)=f(x). Hahn–Banach proves J is an isometry through the dual norm formula, even if U is incomplete. Surjectivity of J is an additional property called reflexivity; it does not hold for every normed space. The closed unit ball is compact in norm exactly in finite-dimensional spaces, a result proved using Riesz’s lemma in infinite dimensions. Weak or weak-star compactness is a different notion and does not imply norm compactness. Duality claims must specify the topology and kind of isomorphism.

similar_questions.prompt: Is the closed unit ball ofℝ³ compact under any norm?
similar_questions.solution: Yes. All finite-dimensional norms are equivalent, and the unit ball is closed and Euclidean-bounded. Heine–Borel gives compactness.

hints: The coefficient sum is evaluation at1, so W₂ is a kernel.
Every polynomial p can be decomposed as[p−p(1)]+p(1).
questions.solution: V has dimension11, with monomial basis1,x,…,x¹⁰. W₂=ker(p↦p(1)) has dimension10. W₁ has dimension6 and contains the constant1, which is not in W₂; thus C fails. Every p∈V decomposes into p−p(1)∈W₂ plus the constant p(1)∈W₁, so W=W₁+W₂=V. Hence B is true and A false. Within W₁ the nonzero evaluation functional has one-dimensional image, so its kernel W₁∩W₂ has dimension6−1=5, proving D. The dimension formula also confirms6+10−5=11.
questions.theory: The smallest subspace containing two subspaces is their sum W₁+W₂={u+v:u∈W₁,v∈W₂}, not generally their union. The formula dim(W₁+W₂)=dimW₁+dimW₂−dim(W₁∩W₂) avoids double-counting the intersection. A polynomial’s coefficient sum equals its value at1, so a zero-sum condition is the kernel of a linear evaluation map. A nonzero linear functional on a finite-dimensional space has rank one and a kernel of codimension one. Restricting that functional to W₁ yields its intersection with W₂; it remains nonzero because1 belongs to W₁. Constants give a convenient complement to the kernel by p=[p−p(1)]+p(1). Remember that degree≤m polynomials have dimension m+1, including the constant and zero polynomial. Independent evaluation conditions generally reduce dimension by their rank, so redundant conditions must not be counted twice.

questions.prompt: Let B be a3×5 matrix overℚ, and suppose {v∈ℝ⁵:Bv=0} has real dimension3. Which statements are true?

options.C: The column span of B has dimension2.

A rational matrix has the same rank overℚ andℝ, since nonzero minors do not change.
questions.solution: Overℝ, rankB=5−3=2. Matrix rank is the maximal order of a nonzero minor; all minors are rational, so the rank overℚ is also2. Rational rank–nullity therefore gives dimℚkerB=5−2=3, proving A. The transpose has rank2 but a3-dimensional domain, so its kernel has dimension1 and B is false. The column span has dimension rankB=2, proving C. The product BBᵀ has rank at most rankB=2, so a3×3 map defined by it is singular and not injective, refuting D. Thus A,C.
questions.theory: Rank–nullity says the dimension of a linear map’s domain equals the rank plus nullity. Rank can be computed by Gaussian elimination or by the largest nonzero minor. Extending the scalar field fromℚ toℝ cannot change which rational determinants are zero, so a rational matrix retains its rank. Nullspace dimensions relative to each field are consequently equal as integers, although the actual sets of rational and real solutions differ. Row rank equals column rank and is unchanged by transposition. For products, rank(AB)≤min(rankA,rankB), immediately ruling out injectivity of a square product with deficient rank. Overℝ, ker(BBᵀ)=ker(Bᵀ) can also be proved from vᵀBBᵀv=‖Bᵀv‖², but the rank bound already settles this question.

options.D: If W₁,W₂ are isomorphic vector spaces, T₁,T₂ have the same characteristic polynomial.

Kernel dimension counts Jordan blocks, while the minimal polynomial records the largest block size.
questions.solution: A is true: if T₂=ST₁S^{−1}, then S restricts to an isomorphism kerT₁→kerT₂. B is false: onℝ⁴ choose T₁=J₃(0)⊕J₁(0) and T₂=J₂(0)⊕J₂(0). D is true even without the kernel hypothesis: every nilpotent operator on d-dimensional V has characteristic polynomialX^d. The question asks for false assertions, so only B is selected.
questions.theory: An operator is nilpotent when some positive power is zero. Its only eigenvalue is zero, its characteristic polynomial in dimension d isX^d, and its minimal polynomial isX^r where r is the least exponent annihilating it. In Jordan form, r is the largest block size, whereas the kernel dimension is the number of Jordan blocks. Equal kernel dimensions therefore do not determine nilpotence indices or similarity classes. Similar operators have identical characteristic and minimal polynomials, and conjugating maps identify their kernels. Isomorphic finite-dimensional real vector spaces only require equal dimensions, a weaker relation than identifying the operators’ actions. A zero operator has full kernel and minimal polynomialX on a nonzero space. Pay attention to “FALSE” in the question: true structural statements must be excluded.

similar_questions.solution: Both act on dimension5 and have two-dimensional kernels. Their characteristic polynomials areX⁵, but their minimal polynomials areX⁴ andX³, so they are not similar.

similar_questions.solution: Every vector is annihilated, so T=0. Its characteristic polynomial isX⁵ and its minimal polynomial isX.

questions.prompt: Let V be real polynomials of degree≤10, including zero, and let T(p)=p′. Which statements are correct?

In the monomial basis its matrix is strictly triangular; repeated differentiation eventually vanishes.
questions.solution: The domain has dimension11, and kerT consists of constants, dimension1. Hence rankT=10, A. Equivalently its image is all degree≤9 polynomials, since every such polynomial has an antiderivative in V. In basis1,x,…,x¹⁰, T(x^k)=kx^{k−1}, so the matrix is strictly upper triangular with all diagonal entries zero. Its determinant and trace are zero, proving B,C. Also T¹¹=0, so for any eigenvector Tp=λp, applying T¹¹ givesλ¹¹p=0 and λ=0. D follows, and all four options are correct.
questions.theory: Differentiation is a linear endomorphism of a finite-degree polynomial space because it lowers degree. The monomial basis makes its matrix triangular, with coefficients1,2,…,m above the main diagonal and zeros on the diagonal. Rank–nullity counts its image from its constant kernel, giving rank m on P_m, whose dimension is m+1. Repeated differentiation makes it nilpotent of index m+1: D^{m+1}=0 but D^m(x^m)=m!≠0 overℝ. Thus its characteristic polynomial isX^{m+1}, all eigenvalues are zero, determinant is zero, and trace is zero. Zero eigenvalues do not imply the operator itself is zero or diagonalizable; the nontrivial nilpotent derivative has substantial rank. Over positive-characteristic fields, derivatives of powers may vanish unexpectedly, so the real-field hypothesis matters.

questions.prompt: Let A be block diagonal with blocks [[e,1],[0,e]] and [[e,1,0],[0,e,0],[0,0,e]]. Which statements are true?

options.A: The algebraic multiplicity of e is5.
options.C: The geometric multiplicity of e is3.

hints: Read the displayed3×3 block carefully: its(2,3) entry is zero.
Subtract eI and count the ranks or kernel dimensions of both blocks.
questions.solution: A is triangular with all five diagonal entries e, so its characteristic polynomial is(X−e)⁵ and the algebraic multiplicity is5, proving A. The2×2 block of A−eI has rank1 and kernel dimension1. The3×3 block has only its(1,2) entry nonzero, so rank1 and kernel dimension2. Therefore rank(A−eI)=2 and dimker(A−eI)=5−2=3, proving C and refuting D. Since the sole eigenspace has dimension3<5, no eigenbasis exists and A is not diagonalizable, proving B. Its minimal polynomial is(X−e)². Thus A,B,C.
questions.theory: The algebraic multiplicity of an eigenvalue is its multiplicity as a root of the characteristic polynomial. Its geometric multiplicity is the dimension of the corresponding eigenspace, computed as nullity(A−λI). For a block diagonal matrix, characteristic polynomials multiply and eigenspace dimensions add across blocks. Geometric multiplicity is at most algebraic multiplicity; equality for every eigenvalue, with splitting of the characteristic polynomial, characterizes diagonalizability. A matrix with only one eigenvalue is diagonalizable only if it is that scalar times the identity. The3×3 block here is not a size-three Jordan block: its second superdiagonal link is zero, so it decomposes as a size-two block and a singleton. Counting matrix size instead of actual links produces the wrong eigenspace dimension.

similar_questions.prompt: For [[3,1,0],[0,3,0],[0,0,3]], find the minimal polynomial and geometric multiplicity.
similar_questions.solution: Subtracting3I gives a nonzero rank-one matrix whose square is zero. Thus the minimal polynomial is(X−3)², and its kernel has dimension3−1=2.

questions.prompt: Let T:ℝ³→ℝ³ satisfy T³−3T²=−2I. Which statements are true?

options.A: There is a basis in which the matrix of T is symmetric.
options.B: There is a basis in which the matrix of T is upper triangular.
options.C: There must be a nonzero v with Tv=v.
options.D: There must be two linearly independent v₁,v₂ with Tvᵢ=vᵢ.

hints: Factor the annihilating polynomial X³−3X²+2.
An annihilating polynomial with distinct real roots forces real diagonalizability, but not the occurrence of every root as an eigenvalue.
questions.solution: The equation says p(T)=0 for p(X)=X³−3X²+2=(X−1)(X²−2X−2). Its roots1,1+√3,1−√3 are distinct and real. The minimal polynomial divides p and therefore splits with no repeated factor; T is diagonalizable overℝ. Its diagonal matrix is both symmetric and upper triangular, proving A,B. C,D are false: T=(1+√3)I satisfies p(T)=0, but T−I=√3I is invertible, so there is no eigenvector with eigenvalue1. An allowed root need not actually appear in the spectrum. Thus A,B.
questions.theory: The minimal polynomial of a linear operator is the monic polynomial of least degree that annihilates it, and it divides every annihilating polynomial. An operator is diagonalizable over a field exactly when its minimal polynomial splits into distinct linear factors over that field. A displayed polynomial identity therefore can prove diagonalizability without finding the characteristic polynomial. Its roots contain the spectrum, but may include values that are not eigenvalues; scalar operators at one permitted root give useful counterexamples to mandatory-eigenvalue claims. A diagonal real matrix is symmetric and triangular, so diagonalizability provides both requested bases. Symmetry in some arbitrary basis does not require symmetry in the original Euclidean coordinates. Repeated roots or nonreal roots in an annihilator would require a more careful argument.

options.B: v₁+v₂+2v₃, v₂+v₃, v₂+3v₃ can be extended to an orthogonal basis of V.

questions.solution: The source omits whether its orthogonal vectors are nonzero. Pairwise orthogonality alone permits zero vectors, whereas some textbook conventions define an orthogonal set to be nonzero. These interpretations give different answer sets, so no unconditional answer is assigned. Under the nonzero convention the vᵢ are independent. A’s coefficient matrix [[1,1,2],[0,1,1],[0,1,3]] has determinant2, and D’s [[1,1,2],[2,1,1],[2,1,3]] has determinant−2; both families extend to a basis. B fails because ⟨v₂+v₃,v₂+3v₃⟩=‖v₂‖²+3‖v₃‖²>0. C fails because its third vector equals twice its first minus its second. Thus the intended answers are A,D. If zero vectors are allowed, choose V=ℝ², v₁=0,v₂=e₁,v₃=e₂; the distinct pairwise orthogonal set satisfies the wording, but every listed triple is dependent. Then no option is guaranteed.
questions.theory: Nonzero pairwise orthogonal vectors in an inner product space are linearly independent: taking the inner product of Σaᵢvᵢ=0 with vⱼ gives aⱼ‖vⱼ‖²=0. The word nonzero is essential in this proof. An independent finite family extends to an algebraic basis, and invertible coefficient matrices preserve its independence. Extension to an orthogonal basis additionally requires the original vectors already be mutually orthogonal; Gram–Schmidt changes vectors and is not an extension retaining them. A zero vector can never belong to a basis. Some texts incorporate nonzeroness into the definition of an orthogonal set, while pairwise orthogonality as a bare condition does not. Source-based grading must state which convention is assumed when it changes the answer. The determinant tests supply the complete intended derivation once nonzero vectors are specified.

questions.solution: The matrices are A=[[6,−13/2],[−13/2,6]], B=[[1,−1/2],[−1/2,2]], C=[[1,−1/2],[−1/2,−2]]. Their determinants are−25/4,7/4,−9/4. Thus A,C each have one positive and one negative eigenvalue, so both have inertia(1,1,0) and are equivalent overℝ, proving B. For B, the leading principal minors1 and7/4 are positive, so it is positive definite, proving C. Therefore A cannot be equivalent to B and C is not positive definite, refuting A,D. Completing squares confirms(b)=(X−Y/2)²+(7/4)Y² and(c)=(X−Y/2)²−(9/4)Y².
questions.theory: A real quadratic form q(x)=xᵀAx uses a symmetric matrix; a cross term bXY corresponds to entries b/2, not b. Two forms are equivalent when an invertible real coordinate change transforms one into the other, equivalently when their matrices are congruent A↦SᵀAS. Sylvester’s law of inertia says the numbers of positive, negative and zero diagonal terms after diagonalization are complete invariants of real congruence. These are different from eigenvalues themselves, which need not be preserved by general congruence. For a symmetric2×2 matrix, a negative determinant forces one positive and one negative eigenvalue. Positive definiteness can be tested by positive leading principal minors, or by completing squares. Overℚ or other fields, matching inertia would not be a complete equivalence criterion; the real-field hypothesis is crucial.

Use the interpolation formula and distinguish “degree n−1” from “degree at most n−1.”
questions.solution: The divided difference is polynomial in z of degree at most n−1, so integration makes P a polynomial of degree at most n−1, with no poles. At z=zⱼ, g(zⱼ)=0 and the integrand reduces to f(ζ)/(ζ−zⱼ); Cauchy’s formula gives P(zⱼ)=f(zⱼ), proving D. Equivalently P(z)=Σⱼf(zⱼ)g(z)/[(z−zⱼ)g′(zⱼ)], the Lagrange interpolating polynomial. A is false by the degree bound; C is false because its apparent node denominators cancel. B asserts exact degree n−1, which is not guaranteed: for n=2 and f≡1, P≡1 has degree0 rather than1, and for f≡0 it is zero. Therefore only D is universally true under the exact printed wording. If B said “at most,” it would also be true.
questions.theory: Lagrange interpolation at n distinct nodes produces the unique polynomial of degree at most n−1 with prescribed node values. Distinctness ensures g′(zⱼ)≠0 and each basis polynomial g(z)/[(z−zⱼ)g′(zⱼ)] equals1 at its own node and0 at the others. A contour representation follows from Cauchy’s formula and residues, provided the data function is holomorphic near the enclosed nodes and contour. The difference quotient of a polynomial is again a polynomial, so apparent singularities atζ=z cancel and the result extends as a polynomial in z. Interpolation does not guarantee exact maximal degree: low-degree or zero data can produce a lower-degree polynomial. The zero polynomial has no usual finite degree. A Part C option with exact degree must be evaluated literally rather than silently inserting “at most.”

questions.prompt: Let D={z∈ℂ:|z|<1}. Consider(a) a holomorphic f:D→D fixing distinct α,β∈D must be the identity; (b) there is no bijective holomorphic map from D to the upper half-plane; (c) a holomorphic f:D→D with f(α)=α and f′(α)=1 must be the identity. Which options are true?

questions.solution: Let φ(z)=(z−α)/(1−conjugate(α)z) and h=φ∘f∘φ^{−1}. Then h:D→D is holomorphic and h(0)=0. In(a), h fixes the nonzero pointφ(β), so equality|h(w)|=|w| in Schwarz’s lemma forces h(z)=cz with|c|=1, and fixing w≠0 gives c=1. Thus f is the identity. In(c), the chain rule at the fixed point gives h′(0)=f′(α)=1; Schwarz’s equality case again gives h(z)=z. Statement(b) is false: F(z)=i(1+z)/(1−z) is a holomorphic bijection onto the upper half-plane, with inverse(w−i)/(w+i) and ImF(z)=(1−|z|²)/|1−z|²>0. Therefore(a),(c) are true and(b) false, so B,D are correct.
questions.theory: Schwarz’s lemma says a holomorphic h:D→D with h(0)=0 satisfies|h(z)|≤|z| and|h′(0)|≤1. Equality at a nonzero point or equality in the derivative bound forces h(z)=cz with|c|=1. To study a fixed point away from zero, conjugate by a disk automorphism; the derivative of the conjugated map at zero equals f′ at the fixed point because the automorphism and inverse derivatives cancel. A second distinct fixed point forces the rotation constant to1, as does derivative1. Möbius transformations map disks and half-planes conformally: the Cayley map supplies a concrete bijection and its inverse. The range must be checked by the sign of the imaginary part, since a changed sign maps to the lower half-plane instead.

similar_questions.prompt: If h:D→D is holomorphic, h(0)=0 and h(1/2)=1/2, determine h.

similar_questions.prompt: Give a biholomorphic map from the upper half-plane to D.
